title: Right Lower Quadrant Abdominal Pain in a Young Woman (Pelvic Inflammatory Disease)
patient_instructions: You are Mary, a 25-year-old woman. For the last 3-4 days you have had a constant, dull ache in the RIGHT LOWER side of your tummy that is slowly getting worse, which worries you. If asked, the pain has always been in that same spot (it did NOT start near your belly button and move) and does not travel anywhere; it is 5/10 and nothing makes it better or worse, including food or position. You feel a bit feverish and nauseated but have not vomited. Your bowels are normal: no diarrhoea, constipation, blood or black stool, no weight or appetite loss. No burning or blood when passing urine. Only if the candidate asks specifically about vaginal symptoms do you volunteer that you have a vaginal discharge - it is yellowish, a little watery and BAD SMELLING. Your last period was 2 weeks ago. If asked a sexual history: you are sexually active, do NOT use condoms, and 'usually have a few partners'. You drink a glass of wine weekly, do not smoke or use drugs, take no medications, have no allergies and are otherwise healthy. Ideas: you worry it might be your appendix or 'something serious'. Concerns: you are scared and want the pain sorted. Expectations: you want it checked and treated. Be initially reticent about the sexual history but answer honestly if asked in a respectful, non-judgemental way. Ask for pain relief if offered.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor in a rural district hospital. Mary, a 25-year-old woman, presents with 3-4 days of right lower quadrant abdominal pain. She is haemodynamically stable. In 8 minutes: take a focused history, then explain your most likely diagnosis and your key differentials to the patient in plain language. You are NOT required to perform a physical examination or state management. Offer analgesia as appropriate during your assessment.
examiner_instructions: Award marks for a structured pain history (SIQORAA/SOCRATES) that specifically establishes NO shift of pain, and for systematically screening grouped differentials: GI (including bowel-cancer red flags), KUB (urinary), and pelvic/gynaecological. The pass-defining move is probing the positive vaginal-discharge finding (colour, consistency, odour), taking a non-judgemental sexual history (condom use, partners, prior STI) and asking the last menstrual period. Candidate should reach pelvic inflammatory disease and give sensible differentials (appendicitis - excluded by no shift; ectopic pregnancy; UTI; hernia). If asked, confirm the patient is stable. Prompt only once: 'Anything else you would like to ask?' Mark communication for empathy, signposting and non-judgemental sexual-history technique.

criteria: Structured SIQORAA/SOCRATES pain history establishing RLQ site with no shift, constant, worsening
Screens grouped differentials - GI red flags, KUB/urinary, pelvic/gynaecological
Elicits positive vaginal discharge and characterises it (yellow, watery, offensive)
Non-judgemental sexual history (condom use, multiple partners, prior STI) and last menstrual period
Offers analgesia and completes SADMA/PMH/FHx as time allows
States pelvic inflammatory disease as most likely with justification from positive findings
Gives relevant differentials with reasoning (appendicitis excluded by absent shift; ectopic pregnancy; UTI; hernia)
Recognises need to exclude pregnancy in a reproductive-age woman
Identifies red flags mandating escalation (peritonism, sepsis, syncope)
Recognises pregnancy must be excluded before empirical antibiotics
Outlines that empirical antibiotics and STI screening/contact tracing will follow (does not need full doses)
Empathy, plain-language explanation avoiding the abbreviation 'PID'
Signposting and non-judgemental approach to sensitive history

red_flags: Signs of peritonism or a surgical abdomen (guarding, rigidity, rebound) suggesting appendicitis, tubo-ovarian abscess or perforation - needs urgent surgical review
Positive pregnancy test / features of ectopic pregnancy (must exclude before doxycycline, Category D)
Sepsis - high fever, tachycardia, hypotension or drowsiness indicating severe PID requiring IV antibiotics and admission
Right upper quadrant pain (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis) suggesting extension of infection
australian_guidelines: Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) mild-moderate PID empirical outpatient regimen: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM/IV single dose PLUS doxycycline 100 mg orally 12-hourly for 14 days PLUS metronidazole 400 mg orally 12-hourly for 14 days; azithromycin 1 g repeated at 1 week if pregnant/breastfeeding or doxycycline non-adherent

Australian STI Management Guidelines (sti.guidelines.org.au, ASHA/ASHM): PID diagnosis, endocervical/vaginal swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, full STI screen (HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B), partner notification/contact tracing and abstinence until treatment complete
RACGP / eTG: exclude pregnancy with urine beta-hCG in any reproductive-age woman with lower abdominal pain before prescribing doxycycline (Category D) and before excluding ectopic pregnancy
PBS-listed ceftriaxone, doxycycline and metronidazole used for empirical PID therapy
learning_objectives: Perform a structured SIQORAA/SOCRATES pain history and use the absence of pain shift to reason against appendicitis
Take a respectful, non-judgemental sexual history and elicit STI risk factors
Recognise pelvic inflammatory disease from lower abdominal pain plus offensive vaginal discharge and STI risk
Understand Australian empirical treatment, STI screening and contact-tracing obligations for PID
key_points: In RLQ pain, always establish whether the pain SHIFTED - a shift suggests appendicitis, no shift keeps PID and pelvic causes high on the list
Any reproductive-age woman with lower abdominal pain needs a urine beta-hCG to exclude ectopic pregnancy before doxycycline
Absence of pain on bimanual examination makes PID unlikely, but the clinical spectrum is wide and many cases have no organism identified
PID sequelae (tubal infertility, ectopic risk, chronic pelvic pain) justify the full 14-day course, adherence advice and partner treatment

citations.claim: A systematic, structured pain history (site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms) is the expected Australian clinical examination standard for this station.
citations.source: Nicholas J Talley, Simon O'Connor - Talley and O'Connor's Clinical Examination (8th edition) - Elsevier Australia (2017).pdf

citations.claim: The station format (candidate tasks, examiner-held performance guidelines, marked history-taking and diagnosis explanation) follows the AMC Handbook of Clinical Assessment condition structure.
Working through grouped differentials (GI, KUB, pelvic) for lower abdominal pain reflects the pocket differential-diagnosis method taught for AMC preparation.
